 © 2026 Yahoo. All rights reserved. Scoot Henderson didn't quite want to call Micah Nori his big brother.
 Not because the relationship isn't close. He just had another way of describing the man tasked with helping him take the next step in his NBA career.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Speaking with The Athletic's Jason Quick, Henderson described it as "an OG (original gangster) kind of relationship."
 It's an interesting description from a 22-year-old guard who's still getting to know his new coach ... especially considering how this season has started.
 The Portland Trail Blazers are 4-1 following Saturday's 112-90 victory over the Utah Jazz. Henderson, meanwhile, has had a considerably tougher time finding his footing.
 His comments about Nori offer an interesting glimpse into how Portland is handling those struggles.
 Quick described Nori as a coach who uses humor to make difficult conversations easier. But there's more to that approach than simply keeping his players comfortable.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Nori isn't afraid to challenge Henderson when things aren't going well. He's encouraged the young guard to stop overthinking possessions and, perhaps more importantly, not let offensive mistakes affect his defense.
 That approach isn't entirely new, either.
 During training camp, Henderson praised Nori's willingness to hold players accountable, explaining that Portland didn't need a coach who would sugarcoat things.
 A coach can believe in a player's talent while still demanding more from his execution. Nori has publicly called Henderson "an elite, elite, basketball player" — but that confidence doesn't erase the areas where his young guard needs to improve.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Saturday offered a pretty clear illustration of both sides.
 Making his first start of the season with Ja Morant sidelined by a hamstring injury, Henderson finished with 14 points and three steals in 31 minutes. He also shot 4-for-11, recorded one assist and committed four turnovers.
 The scoring and defensive activity were encouraging. The ball security and playmaking? Not so much.
 Those are precisely the inconsistencies Nori has to help Henderson work through.
 Portland isn't in the same position it was when Henderson arrived as the No. 3 overall pick in 2023. The Blazers are trying to win games now, and a backcourt featuring Damian Lillard and Jrue Holiday gives Nori experienced alternatives when mistakes pile up.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement But Henderson can't spend every possession worrying about his next mistake, either.
 That's the balance Nori has to find — holding Henderson accountable without coaching the aggression out of him.
 It requires more than encouraging quotes after games. It requires trust when the turnovers come, when the jumper isn't falling and when the right decision becomes harder to recognize in real time.
 Henderson's description suggests the two are developing exactly that kind of relationship.
 He knows there's work to be done, too.
 "I'm not going back down from the challenge," Henderson told Quick.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement That's the attitude Portland needs from him. But confidence and production are two different things, and Henderson still has to translate those words into more consistent basketball.
 Nori can't make the right read for Henderson or prevent every turnover. What he can do is help ensure those mistakes become lessons rather than reasons to hesitate.
 Henderson already knows his coach believes in him. That's never been the issue.
 The real challenge is translating that trust into better decisions when the game speeds up. Nori can offer all the guidance in the world — but what Henderson does with it will ultimately determine how far this relationship takes him.
